newsitem.title: UK: Lockheed raises sights on cost-cutting.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed raises sights on cost-cutting.

text.p: Lockheed Martin Corp believes it can now cut its costs by at least another $200 million on top of the $2.4 billion it has predicted it can achieve from its recent spate of defence mergers and acquisitions.
Earlier this year the company said its consolidation plan was on schedule to have cut $2.4 billion off its annual costs by between 1993 and the end of the decade.

"We now believe that number is closer to $2.6 billion," president and chief operating officer Vance Coffman told Reuters in an interview. He was speaking ahead of Britain's Farnborough International air show, which opens on Monday.

Coffman said the savings, which amount to around 10 percent of sales, would cut prices for existing customers where it operates on cost-plus contracts, namely the U.S. government, and give it a greater edge in the market at home and overseas.

"Because the cost-plus business is a large part of our business base these savings go immediately to our customers," Coffman said. "It leaves us in an excellent position in competing for new contracts."

After a rapid series of mergers and acquisitions since 1992, Lockheed was now concentrating on rationalising its businesses and working off its debt, leaving any further major consolidation in the U.S. defence business to others.
"I cannot tell you what the next step would be but I don't think it's over," he said.
"As far as Lockheed Martin is concerned we are in a stage of looking for at the most, niche-type acquisitions," he said.
But the next major move for Lockheed is likely to be in selling off non-core businesses.

Coffman said the company has identified potential disposals representing $2.0 billion of current group sales, not including a surplus property portfolio, and further announcements should be forthcoming by late November.
The company currently has total debt of around $12 billion leaving it with a debt to equity gearing of over 60 percent.
But Coffman said strong cash flows meant Lockheed expects to cut its gearing to below 40 percent by the year 2000.

"We believe we can have our debt down to below 40 percent (gearing) in the next three to four years ... I would think the mid-30s," he said. "We have said we expect to generate somewhere between $8-10 billion of cash in the next five years and these projections are on track."

He added that the company was also on target to see sales grow to between $28 and 29 billion in the current year from $22.9 billion last year and to over $30 billion next year, but these forecasts are before any disposals.

In the last four years Lockheed has acquired the General Dynamics fighter aircraft division, merged with Martin Marietta in a $10 billion deal announced just before the last Farnborough air show two years ago, and bought much of Loral Corp for $9.1 billion earlier this year.
